title: Two-Way Doors
summary:
A **two-way door** is a decision you can reverse cheaply if it turns out wrong, typically anything that varies with scale: instance counts and sizes, cache TTLs, whether a module runs in-process or as its own service, which queue or cache you use behind a clean interface.

Apply **minimalism** here: do the simplest thing that works today, because you can change it when scale demands.

The key technique is **decouple the components, but delay the split**. Keep clean boundaries in the code (modules that talk through explicit interfaces and own their own data), yet deploy them together as one unit. When growth finally requires separation, splitting a module out becomes a change in *physical deployment shape* (an in-process call becomes an RPC), not a rewrite of the architecture.

The condition is real: the door only stays two-way if the boundaries are honest. If modules reach into each other's tables or share global state, splitting later is a rewrite and the door has quietly become one-way.

So: a team of five at a few thousand requests per second does not need twelve microservices and a service mesh. It needs a well-structured [modular monolith](#/sd/f/scalable-simplicity) with clean seams, plus a careful look at the real [one-way doors](#/sd/f/one-way-door): the API, data flow and data model.

drills.q: A team of five serves about 2,000 requests per second. A teammate proposes 12 microservices connected by Kafka "so we can scale later". What is the better plan?
options: Agree: splitting later is impossible, so split now
Build a modular monolith with explicit module interfaces and per-module data ownership; extract services only when a module needs independent scaling or ownership
Build one big ball of code and refactor when it hurts
Use microservices only for the database layer
drills.explain: Process layout is a two-way door when boundaries are clean, so pay for distribution only when scale demands it. A big ball of code is the opposite mistake: it turns the later split into a rewrite.

drills.q: Which conditions keep a module cheap to extract into its own service later? Select all that apply.
options: Other modules call it only through its public interface
It owns its tables; no other module queries them directly
It lives in a separate Git repository from day one
It does not depend on in-memory global state shared with other modules
drills.explain: Interface-only access, data ownership and no hidden shared state are what make extraction a deployment change. A separate repo is neither necessary nor sufficient; it adds overhead without creating a boundary.

drills.q: Which of these is most clearly a two-way door?
options: The ID format exposed in public URLs
The TTL of an internal cache entry
The wire format of events consumed by other teams
Which fields a public webhook payload contains
drills.explain: A TTL is a config value that can be changed with a deploy and no external effect. The other three are published contracts that others have built on.

drills.q: Order the steps to extract a module from a modular monolith into its own service.
items: Make all callers use the module's interface, with no direct table access
Give the module its own schema or database
Replace the in-process call behind the interface with an RPC client
Deploy the module separately and shift traffic gradually
drills.explain: Boundaries and data ownership are prepared first, while everything is still in one process and easy to test. Only then does the call become remote; deploying last lets you shift traffic and roll back.

drills.q: What does "decouple the components but delay the split" mean, and what makes it fail?
drills.answer: Keep clean module boundaries (interfaces, owned data) inside one deployable so that later separation only changes deployment shape. It fails when modules share tables or global state, because then splitting becomes a rewrite and the two-way door has turned into a one-way door.
